result.note: Tests the February 2026 easing of post-2020 curbs on Chinese suppliers for power-transmission equipment and the 2030 non-fossil capacity goal.

questions.prompt: In February 2026, India began easing restrictions on Chinese suppliers in public procurement. Consider the following statements:
items: The restrictions, imposed after a 2020 border clash, required Chinese bidders on public contracts to register with a government committee and secure political and security clearances.
Under the easing, state-run firms can import critical power-transmission components from China without the standard government clearance.
The easing responds to a projected 40% shortfall in transformers and reactors over the next three years.
questions.ask: How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explain: All three statements match the story. The 2020 curbs had effectively locked Chinese firms out of a government contract market estimated at over USD 700 billion, and the government has framed the change as a targeted waiver.
questions.source: State-run firms can now import critical power-transmission components from China without the standard government “Mother May I.”

questions.prompt: Reporting on India's February 2026 easing of curbs on Chinese power equipment cited a national goal for non-fossil power capacity by 2030. What is that goal?
questions.explain: The story gives India's 2030 goal as 500 GW of non-fossil capacity. It says this goal is hard to meet without Chinese transformers and reactors.
questions.source: Without the Chinese hardware, the 2030 goal of 500 GW non-fossil capacity is little more than a pipe dream.
